claim: Self-reported nutrition intake (NI) data are prone to reporting bias that may induce bias in estimands in nutrition studies.
source: Self-reported nutrition intake (NI) data are prone to reporting bias that may induce bias in estimands in nutrition studies; however, they are used anyway due to high feasibility.
evidence: This is a general statement about self-reported nutrition data that is supported by established scientific knowledge and is referenced throughout the manuscript with citations.

claim: Self-reported nutrition intake data are used in nutrition studies due to high feasibility.
source: Self-reported nutrition intake (NI) data are prone to reporting bias that may induce bias in estimands in nutrition studies; however, they are used anyway due to high feasibility.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field and is a commonly accepted reason for using self-report methods.

claim: In the IDATA study, significant bias in mean NI was removed with Goldberg cutoffs when 120 among 303 participants were excluded.
source: Using the Interactive Diet and Activity Tracking in the American Association of Retired Persons (IDATA) data, significant bias in mean NI was removed with Goldberg cutoffs (120 among 303 participants excluded).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by empirical data analysis from the IDATA study as reported in the manuscript.

claim: Sample size in IDATA was insufficient to evaluate bias reductions in associations between NI and health outcomes.
source: Associations between NI and health outcomes (weight, waist circumference, heart rate, systolic/diastolic blood pressure, and VO2 max) were estimated, but sample size was insufficient to evaluate bias reductions.
evidence: This is an inference made by the authors based on their analysis of the IDATA data and the wide confidence intervals observed.

claim: Significant bias in simulated associations using self-reported NI was reduced but not completely eliminated by Goldberg cutoffs in 14 of 24 nutrition-outcome pairs.
source: Significant bias in simulated associations using self-reported NI was reduced but not completely eliminated by Goldberg cutoffs in 14 of 24 nutrition-outcome pairs; bias was not reduced for the remaining 10 cases.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data generated and analyzed in the study.

claim: Bias was not reduced by Goldberg cutoffs for 10 of 24 nutrition-outcome pairs in simulated data.
source: Significant bias in simulated associations using self-reported NI was reduced but not completely eliminated by Goldberg cutoffs in 14 of 24 nutrition-outcome pairs; bias was not reduced for the remaining 10 cases.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data generated and analyzed in the study.

claim: 95% coverage probabilities were improved by applying Goldberg cutoffs in most cases but underperformed compared with biomarker data.
source: Also, 95% coverage probabilities were improved by applying Goldberg cutoffs in most cases but underperformed compared with biomarker data.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results showing coverage probability metrics.

claim: Goldberg cutoffs may achieve bias elimination in estimating mean NI.
source: Although Goldberg cutoffs may achieve bias elimination in estimating mean NI, bias in estimates of associations between NI and outcomes will not necessarily be reduced or eliminated after application of Goldberg cutoffs.
evidence: This claim is supported by both empirical data analysis and simulation results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Bias in estimates of associations between NI and outcomes will not necessarily be reduced or eliminated after application of Goldberg cutoffs.
source: Although Goldberg cutoffs may achieve bias elimination in estimating mean NI, bias in estimates of associations between NI and outcomes will not necessarily be reduced or eliminated after application of Goldberg cutoffs.
evidence: This claim is supported by both empirical data analysis and simulation results showing incomplete bias reduction.

claim: Whether one uses Goldberg cutoffs should be decided based on research purposes and not general rules.
source: Whether one uses Goldberg cutoffs should therefore be decided based on research purposes and not general rules.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings of the study, representing an inference from the data.

claim: Biomarker approaches are considered more accurate compared with self-report for measuring nutrition intake.
source: Biomarker approaches are considered more accurate compared with self-report; however, they are typically expensive and require special equipment for each nutrient.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of nutrition research.

claim: Biomarker approaches are typically expensive and require special equipment for each nutrient.
source: Biomarker approaches are considered more accurate compared with self-report; however, they are typically expensive and require special equipment for each nutrient.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the practical limitations of biomarker methods.

claim: Self-report approaches are less expensive and do not require special laboratory equipment or techniques.
source: Self-report approaches are less expensive and do not require special laboratory equipment or techniques, and can be applied to the measurement of any nutrition components from macronutrients (i.e. carbohydrates, fat, and protein) to micronutrients (i.e. minerals and vitamins); however, self-reported data are known to be fraught with bias (Schoeller et al., 1990; Dhurandhar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the practical advantages of self-report methods.

claim: Self-report approaches can be applied to the measurement of any nutrition components from macronutrients to micronutrients.
source: Self-report approaches are less expensive and do not require special laboratory equipment or techniques, and can be applied to the measurement of any nutrition components from macronutrients (i.e. carbohydrates, fat, and protein) to micronutrients (i.e. minerals and vitamins); however, self-reported data are known to be fraught with bias (Schoeller et al., 1990; Dhurandhar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the versatility of self-report methods.

claim: Self-reported data are known to be fraught with bias.
source: Self-report approaches are less expensive and do not require special laboratory equipment or techniques, and can be applied to the measurement of any nutrition components from macronutrients (i.e. carbohydrates, fat, and protein) to micronutrients (i.e. minerals and vitamins); however, self-reported data are known to be fraught with bias (Schoeller et al., 1990; Dhurandhar et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Energy intake (EI) is defined as a sum of the total metabolizable energy content of consumed foods and beverages.
source: Energy intake (EI) is defined as a sum of the total metabolizable energy content of consumed foods and beverages (Astrup, 2005).
evidence: This is a definition supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: EI can be measured using biomarkers, especially by energy balance approaches in which respiratory gas analysis or doubly labeled water (DLW) are used for the calculation of energy expenditure (EE).
source: EI can be measured using biomarkers, especially by energy balance approaches in which respiratory gas analysis or doubly labeled water (DLW) are used for the calculation of energy expenditure (EE) (Ferrannini, 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to established methodology.

claim: EI can be calculated using EE accounting for change in energy stores during the period of measurement.
source: EI can be calculated using EE accounting for change in energy stores (i.e. body composition) during the period of measurement.
evidence: This is established methodology in energy balance research.

claim: Respiratory gas analysis typically requires the participants to wear a gas mask or stay in a metabolic chamber.
source: The respiratory gas analysis typically requires the participants to wear a gas mask or stay in a metabolic chamber (Leonard, 2012), which restricts participants' behavior; thus, the measured EI using the respiratory gas analysis may not reflect EI from habitual eating behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation describing the methodology.

claim: Respiratory gas analysis restricts participants' behavior, thus the measured EI using respiratory gas analysis may not reflect EI from habitual eating behavior.
source: The respiratory gas analysis typically requires the participants to wear a gas mask or stay in a metabolic chamber (Leonard, 2012), which restricts participants' behavior; thus, the measured EI using the respiratory gas analysis may not reflect EI from habitual eating behavior.
evidence: This is an inference based on the methodological constraints of respiratory gas analysis.

claim: DLW requires the participants to visit the laboratory to drink labeled water enriched with stable hydrogen and oxygen isotopes and collect urine for measurement of isotope levels.
source: DLW requires the participants to visit the laboratory to drink labeled water enriched with stable hydrogen and oxygen isotopes and collect urine for measurement of isotope levels.
evidence: This is established methodology for DLW measurement.

claim: DLW is considered to reflect habitual eating behavior and widely accepted as a standard and reliable approach in measuring EI in free-living individuals.
source: It is considered to reflect habitual eating behavior and widely accepted as a standard and reliable approach in measuring EI in free-living individuals (Schoeller et al., 1986; Speakman, 1997; Schoeller and van Santen, 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Given the high cost of isotopes and laboratories to analyze collected urine, DLW is not practical in large-scale epidemiological surveillance.
source: However, given the high cost of isotopes and laboratories to analyze collected urine, DLW is not practical in large-scale epidemiological surveillance (Banna et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge about the practical limitations of DLW.

claim: EISR is biased compared with the EI measured by biomarker such as DLW (EIBIO).
source: However, EISR is biased compared with the EI measured by biomarker such as DLW (EIBIO) (Schoeller et al., 1990) and is discouraged from use to estimate actual EI (Dhurandhar et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: EISR is discouraged from use to estimate actual EI.
source: However, EISR is biased compared with the EI measured by biomarker such as DLW (EIBIO) (Schoeller et al., 1990) and is discouraged from use to estimate actual EI (Dhurandhar et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: EISR is computed from the information of reported foods and beverages using tables of food and beverage nutrients, composed of weights, calories, and the amount of macro- and micronutrients.
source: For example, EISR is computed from the information of reported foods and beverages using tables of food and beverage nutrients, composed of weights, calories, and the amount of macro- and micronutrients.
evidence: This describes the established methodology for computing EISR.

claim: Compositions of foods and beverages are different among brands, stores, and seasons.
source: Compositions of foods and beverages are different among brands, stores, and seasons (Martelli et al., 2018), and thus nutrient databases cannot be exhaustive.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Nutrient databases cannot be exhaustive.
source: Compositions of foods and beverages are different among brands, stores, and seasons (Martelli et al., 2018), and thus nutrient databases cannot be exhaustive.
evidence: This is an inference based on the variability in food composition.

claim: EISR using nutrient databases may not be accurate.
source: Consequently, EISR using such databases may not be accurate (McHenry et al., 1945).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and is an inference from the limitations of nutrient databases.

claim: Social desirability is associated with reporting bias.
source: Further factors, including social desirability (i.e. people do not want to be seen as a 'big eater' in general) (Heymsfield et al., 1995) and weight/social status (Heymsfield et al., 1995; Johansson et al., 1998; Macdiarmid and Blundell, 1998; Johansson et al., 2001; Klesges et al., 1995), are known to be associated with reporting bias.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Weight/social status is associated with reporting bias.
source: Further factors, including social desirability (i.e. people do not want to be seen as a 'big eater' in general) (Heymsfield et al., 1995) and weight/social status (Heymsfield et al., 1995; Johansson et al., 1998; Macdiarmid and Blundell, 1998; Johansson et al., 2001; Klesges et al., 1995), are known to be associated with reporting bias.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The difference between EIBIO and EISR is due to systemic biases rather than a random error.
source: Thus, the difference between EIBIO and EISR is due to systemic biases rather than a random error.
evidence: This is an inference based on the factors contributing to reporting bias discussed in the manuscript.

claim: Self-report approaches have been predominantly used in large-scale nutrition epidemiology due to their high feasibility.
source: Despite concerns about the accuracy of self-report approaches, they have been predominantly used in large-scale nutrition epidemiology due to their high feasibility.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the use of self-report methods in epidemiology.

claim: One approach to mitigate bias is to exclude those reporting EISR out of the range considered by the researchers to be plausible, such as from 500 to 3500 kcal/day.
source: For example, one approach is to exclude those reporting EISR out of the range considered by the researchers to be plausible, such as from 500 to 3500 kcal/day (Banna et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation describing this approach.

claim: The rule to exclude EISR from 500 to 3500 kcal/day does not consider individual variability and is not appropriate for those whose intake is truly above 3500 kcal/day, such as elite athletes or those whose body size is large.
source: However, this rule does not consider individual variability and is not appropriate for those whose intake is truly above 3500 kcal/day, such as elite athletes or those whose body size is large and requires more than 3500 kcal/day to maintain their weight (Santos et al., 2014; DeLany et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of fixed cutoff rules, supported by citations.

claim: Other approaches use EE prediction equations to account for individual variability in EI.
source: Other approaches are to use EE prediction equations to account for individual variability in EI (McCrory et al., 2002; Huang et al., 2005; Vinken et al., 1999; Livingstone and Robson, 2000; Xie et al., 2003; Briefel et al., 1995; Huang et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: If the EE predicted considering various factors is far from EISR, those individuals are considered under/overreporting their actual EI.
source: If the EE predicted considering various factors (e.g. age, weight, sex) is far from EISR, those individuals are considered under/overreporting their actual EI.
evidence: This describes the logic behind EE prediction approaches.

claim: EE prediction approaches have evidently reduced misclassification.
source: Indeed, such an approach has evidently reduced misclassification (Tooze et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The Goldberg cutoffs have been used in nutrition epidemiology to assess nutritional status in specific populations and investigate the association between nutritional status and health and socioeconomic outcomes.
source: Among proposed approaches, the Goldberg cutoffs Goldberg et al., 1991 have been used in nutrition epidemiology to assess nutritional status in specific populations and investigate the association between nutritional status and health and socioeconomic outcomes (Livingstone and Robson, 2000; Xie et al., 2003; Briefel et al., 1995; Huang et al., 2004; Martin et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The rationale of using the Goldberg cutoffs to exclude data from individuals considered to have unreliable EISR is based on an assumption that if total EI is underestimated, it is probable that the intakes of other nutrients are also underestimated.
source: Therefore, the rationale of using the Goldberg cutoffs (and other similar approaches) to exclude data from individuals considered to have unreliable EISR is based on an assumption, 'if total EI is underestimated, it is probable that the intakes of other nutrients are also underestimated' (Livingstone and Black, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation describing the rationale.

claim: In a previous study, the authors demonstrated that the Goldberg cutoffs do not necessarily eliminate the bias in estimating the associations between EI and various health outcomes.
source: In our previous study, we demonstrated that the Goldberg cutoffs do not necessarily eliminate the bias in estimating the associations between EI and various health outcomes (Ejima et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: More than 90% of the IDATA participants are non-Hispanic whites.
source: More than 90% of the participants are non-Hispanic whites, and their mean age was 63.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the IDATA dataset.

claim: The mean age of IDATA participants was 63.
source: More than 90% of the participants are non-Hispanic whites, and their mean age was 63.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the IDATA dataset.

claim: The mean BMI of IDATA participants was 27.7 kg/m2.
source: The mean BMI was 27.7 kg/m2, and 30% had obesity (BMI ≥30).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the IDATA dataset.

claim: 30% of IDATA participants had obesity (BMI ≥30).
source: The mean BMI was 27.7 kg/m2, and 30% had obesity (BMI ≥30).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the IDATA dataset.

claim: There was significant mean underreporting in which the biomarker nutrition intakes (NIBIO) was greater than the self-reported nutrition intakes (NISR) in all four types of nutrition intake.
source: There was significant mean underreporting in which the biomarker nutrition intakes (NIBIO) was greater than the self-reported nutrition intakes (NISR) in all four types of nutrition intake (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Table 2.

claim: By the Goldberg cutoffs, 120 among 303 participants were excluded (40%).
source: By the Goldberg cutoffs, 120 among 303 participants were excluded (40%) (Table 3).
evidence: This is a result from applying the Goldberg cutoffs to the IDATA dataset.

claim: There was significant underreporting in the rejected cases.
source: There was significant underreporting in the rejected cases, whereas reporting bias (NISR – NIBIO) was not significant in the accepted cases in all four NI.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis of the IDATA dataset.

claim: Reporting bias (NISR – NIBIO) was not significant in the accepted cases in all four NI.
source: There was significant underreporting in the rejected cases, whereas reporting bias (NISR – NIBIO) was not significant in the accepted cases in all four NI.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis of the IDATA dataset.

claim: The difference in the biases between the accepted and the rejected cases was significant.
source: Further, the difference in the biases between the accepted and the rejected cases was significant.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical testing of the IDATA data.

claim: The mean NISR in the accepted cases was significantly larger than that in the rejected cases in all four NI.
source: The mean NISR in the accepted cases was significantly larger than that in the rejected cases in all four NI.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis of the IDATA dataset.

claim: NIBIO was significantly larger in the rejected cases in sodium intake (SI).
source: NIBIO was significantly larger in the rejected cases in sodium intake (SI), whereas it was comparable between those groups in energy intake (EI), potassium intake (PoI), and protein intake (PrI).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis of the IDATA dataset.

claim: NIBIO was comparable between accepted and rejected cases in energy intake (EI), potassium intake (PoI), and protein intake (PrI).
source: NIBIO was significantly larger in the rejected cases in sodium intake (SI), whereas it was comparable between those groups in energy intake (EI), potassium intake (PoI), and protein intake (PrI).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis of the IDATA dataset.

claim: The bias was significantly and negatively correlated with NIBIO.
source: The bias was significantly and negatively correlated with NIBIO (Figure 1 top panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The means of accepted cases of NISR correspond to the mean of NIBIO better than the mean of NISR in the rejected cases.
source: The means of accepted cases of NISR correspond to the mean of NIBIO better than the mean of NISR in the rejected cases (Figure 1 bottom panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The Goldberg cutoffs reduce (and may eliminate) the bias in mean NISR by identifying predominantly underreporting individuals.
source: These findings suggest that the Goldberg cutoffs reduce (and may eliminate) the bias in mean NISR by identifying predominantly underreporting individuals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the empirical data analysis.

claim: The difference in self-reported nutrition intake between accepted and rejected cases is predominantly from differences in reporting and less so from differences in actual biomarker-measured intake.
source: The difference in self-reported nutrition intake between accepted and rejected cases is predominantly from differences in reporting and less so from differences in actual biomarker-measured intake.
evidence: This is an inference based on the empirical data analysis.

claim: The associations between EIBIO, SIBIO, and PrIBIO and WC were statistically significant.
source: The associations between EIBIO, SIBIO, and PrIBIO and WC were statistically significant (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in the figures and supplementary file.

claim: PoIBIO was significantly associated with VO2.
source: PoIBIO was significantly associated with VO2.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis of the IDATA dataset.

claim: The percent bias (b) was significantly below 0% (underestimation) in only limited cases (EI and BW, and EI and WC).
source: The percent bias (b) was significantly below 0% (underestimation) in only limited cases (EI and BW, and EI and WC) and we could not conclude whether the bias exists or not for the rest of the cases.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis of the IDATA dataset.

claim: Significant overestimation (b>0) was not observed in any cases.
source: Significant overestimation (b>0) was not observed in any cases (the left panel in Figure 2 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2 and supplementary file.

claim: The bias was reduced (|r|<100) but remained (r≠0) for the association between EI and BW, and between EI and WC.
source: The bias was reduced (|r|<100) but remained (r≠0) for the association between EI and BW, and between EI and WC.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis of the IDATA dataset.

claim: The bias for all biomarker simulations was close to 0.
source: The bias for all biomarker simulations was close to 0 (red squares in the bias column of Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3.

claim: For the cases with positive correlation, the positive bias in βNISR,HO was observed, and for the cases with negative correlation, the negative bias in βNISR,HO was observed, suggesting that the self-reported data cause attenuation bias.
source: For the cases with positive correlation, the positive bias in βNISR,HO was observed, and for the cases with negative correlation, the negative bias in βNISR,HO was observed, suggesting that the self-reported data cause attenuation bias (i.e. |βNISR,HO|<|βNIBIO,HO|) as observed in many studies (Kipnis et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results and is consistent with previous research cited.

claim: After application of the Goldberg cutoffs, the bias was reduced in 14 among 24 combinations of NI and HO.
source: After application of the Goldberg cutoffs, the bias was reduced in 14 among 24 combinations of NI and HO, which can be seen in Figure 3 where the green circles are closer to 0 than the blue triangles.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3.

claim: The bias was reduced in all six outcomes and reduction was large when EI is used as a predictor.
source: Specifically, |βNIG,HO|<|βNISR,HO|. Notably, the bias was reduced in all six outcomes and reduction was large when EI is used as a predictor.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claim: When SI, PoI, and PrI are used as predictors, the bias was not much changed by applying the Goldberg cutoffs.
source: When SI, PoI, and PrI are used as predictors, the bias was not much changed by applying the Goldberg cutoffs (green circles and blue triangles are close to each other in the bias column of Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3.

claim: In most cases, the MSE was smaller for NIBIO compared with NISR, and the MSE for NISR became smaller after applying the Goldberg cutoffs.
source: In most cases, the MSE was also smaller for NIBIO compared with NISR, and the MSE for NISR became smaller after applying the Goldberg cutoffs (green circles are often closer to 0 than the blue triangles in the MSE column of Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3.

claim: The coverage probabilities (CP) were close to 95% when NIBIO was used as a predictor.
source: The coverage probabilities (CP) were close to 95% when NIBIO was used as a predictor, as was expected, whereas it was mostly lower than 95% when NISR was used.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claim: Coverage probability was mostly lower than 95% when NISR was used.
source: The coverage probabilities (CP) were close to 95% when NIBIO was used as a predictor, as was expected, whereas it was mostly lower than 95% when NISR was used.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claim: The coverage probability increased by applying Goldberg cutoffs; however, it is still lower than 95% in most cases.
source: The coverage probability increased by applying Goldberg cutoffs (green circles are often closer to 95 than the blue triangles in the CP column of Figure 3); however, it is still lower than 95% in most cases.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3.

claim: Biases were not affected by varying η for the range of values considered.
source: Biases were not affected by varying η for the range of values we considered, suggesting that error in health outcomes (or variance in health outcomes which cannot be explained by variance in biomarker-based nutrition intake) does not influence NI-HO association estimations where NI is used as an independent variable.
evidence: This claim is supported by sensitivity analysis results.

claim: Error in health outcomes does not influence NI-HO association estimations where NI is used as an independent variable.
source: Biases were not affected by varying η for the range of values we considered, suggesting that error in health outcomes (or variance in health outcomes which cannot be explained by variance in biomarker-based nutrition intake) does not influence NI-HO association estimations where NI is used as an independent variable.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sensitivity analysis results.

claim: Bias was negative when self-reported data (NISR or NIG) were used under the default value of σ, and the magnitude of bias increased as σ increased.
source: Bias was negative when self-reported data (NISR or NIG) were used under the default value of σ, and the magnitude of bias increased as σ increased (i.e., the association was attenuated).
evidence: This claim is supported by sensitivity analysis results.

claim: When the error is extremely small (e.g. σ=0.25), the bias becomes positive, which is because the mean error function (µ) was negative at low NI and positive at high NI, thus the association was intensified.
source: However, when the error is extremely small (e.g. σ=0.25 in Figure 3—figure supplement 2), the bias becomes positive, which is because the mean error function (µ) was negative at low NI and positive at high NI, thus the association was intensified.
evidence: This claim is supported by sensitivity analysis results and represents an inference about the mechanism.

claim: Whether or not the bias becomes positive or negative is determined by the balance between the mean error function and random error.
source: Whether or not the bias becomes positive or negative is determined by the balance between the mean error function and random error.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sensitivity analysis results.

claim: Reporting bias in self-reported nutrition intake was demonstrated using both empirical data analysis and a simulation study.
source: In this study, reporting bias in self-reported nutrition intake was demonstrated using both empirical data analysis and a simulation study.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the study's findings.

claim: The bias in mean self-reported nutrition intake was eliminated by applying Goldberg cutoffs to exclude extreme reporters (mostly under-reporters).
source: We confirmed the bias in mean self-reported nutrition intake was eliminated by applying Goldberg cutoffs to exclude extreme reporters (mostly under-reporters).
evidence: This claim is supported by empirical data analysis.

claim: This bias can be mostly explained by differences in reporting between the accepted and rejected cases rather than a difference in actual nutrition intake between the accepted and rejected cases.
source: This bias can be mostly explained by differences in reporting between the accepted and rejected cases rather than a difference in actual nutrition intake between the accepted and rejected cases.
evidence: This is an inference based on the empirical data analysis.

claim: The significant bias for the associations between EI and BW and the association between EI and WC were reduced but remained after applying Goldberg cutoffs.
source: The significant bias for the associations between EI and BW and the association between EI and WC were reduced but remained after applying Goldberg cutoffs.
evidence: This claim is supported by empirical data analysis.

claim: Significant bias in associations for other nutrition-outcome pairs was not observed, and therefore conclusions cannot be made regarding the utility of applying the Goldberg cutoffs to reduce bias for these associations in the empirical data.
source: We did not observe significant bias in associations for other nutrition-outcome pairs, and therefore cannot make conclusions regarding the utility of applying the Goldberg cutoffs to reduce bias for these associations in the empirical data.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the empirical analysis.

claim: The existence of bias in estimated associations when the self-reported data were used was confirmed in the simulation study.
source: We confirmed the existence of bias in estimated associations when the self-reported data were used, and these biases were reduced, but not eliminated, by applying the Goldberg cutoffs in general.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claim: Biases in estimated associations were reduced, but not eliminated, by applying the Goldberg cutoffs in general.
source: We confirmed the existence of bias in estimated associations when the self-reported data were used, and these biases were reduced, but not eliminated, by applying the Goldberg cutoffs in general.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claim: Large MSE and low coverage probability were confirmed when self-reported data were used.
source: We also confirmed large MSE and low coverage probability when self-reported data were used; MSE and low coverage probability were improved by using Goldberg cutoffs, but were not recovered to the levels of biomarker data.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claim: MSE and low coverage probability were improved by using Goldberg cutoffs, but were not recovered to the levels of biomarker data.
source: We also confirmed large MSE and low coverage probability when self-reported data were used; MSE and low coverage probability were improved by using Goldberg cutoffs, but were not recovered to the levels of biomarker data.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claim: The empirical data analyses and the simulation study suggest that the Goldberg cutoffs improve the estimates in nutrition-health outcome associations; however, the biases were not completely removed.
source: Overall, the empirical data analyses and the simulation study suggest that the Goldberg cutoffs improve the estimates in nutrition-health outcome associations; however, the biases were not completely removed.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on both empirical and simulation results.

claim: The study investigated three other nutrition intakes (sodium, potassium, and protein) in addition to energy intake.
source: First, although energy intake has traditionally been studied more with respect to Goldberg cutoffs, herein we also investigated three other nutrition intakes: sodium, potassium, and protein.
evidence: This describes the scope of the study.

claim: The Goldberg cutoffs are believed to reduce the bias in nutrition intake broadly.
source: However, given that the Goldberg cutoffs are believed to reduce the bias in nutrition intake broadly, we expanded the approach to these other nutrition intakes, which can be measured by biomarkers (Livingstone and Black, 2003).
evidence: This is a statement about the general belief regarding Goldberg cutoffs, supported by a citation.

claim: The data generation process was based on the IDATA dataset.
source: The data generation process was based on the IDATA dataset.
evidence: This describes the methodology of the simulation study.

claim: The simulation was able to generate datasets reflective of those that would be seen in the real world.
source: Thus, we were able to simulate datasets reflective of those that would be seen in the real world.
evidence: This is an inference about the validity of the simulation approach.

claim: In the analysis of IDATA, only bivariate associations for nutrition-health outcomes were used.
source: In the analysis of IDATA, we used only bivariate associations for nutrition-health outcomes.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the empirical analysis.

claim: Including various covariates or different models may influence the existence or lack of bias in nutrition-health associations.
source: It is possible that including various covariates or different models may influence the existence or lack of bias in nutrition-health associations.
evidence: This is speculation about potential limitations of the study.

claim: The reporting bias was set to be normally distributed in the data-generation process for the simulations.
source: The reporting bias was set to be normally distributed.
evidence: This describes an assumption in the simulation methodology.

claim: Modeling the bias using other distributions may improve model fit and generate more realistic data.
source: Modeling the bias using other distributions (such as a heavier tailed distribution that may be more consistent with a zero-bounded intake) may improve model fit, and thus generated more realistic data.
